summary: This standards-track memo defines how to carry SMPTE ST 291-1 ancillary data over the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). Ancillary data in professional video holds extras such as captions and timing information, alongside the picture. The payload format lets it be sent across IP networks as part of professional video workflows.

plainLanguage.summary: A TV picture comes with extra hidden notes, like subtitles. This is a way to mail those notes over the internet along with the picture.

subtitle: How to carry the captions, time code and other hidden extras of professional video inside RTP packets.

tldr.problem: Professional video on serial digital interfaces (SDI) carries ancillary data such as time code, Closed Captioning and Active Format Description outside the visible picture, and that data needs a way to travel over IP networks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8331 defines an RTP payload format that packs SMPTE ST 291-1 ancillary (ANC) data packets with their line, horizontal offset and stream information, so a receiver can put them back where they came from. It also registers the video/smpte291 media type and its SDP parameters.
tldr.outcome: ANC data can travel alone or next to an RTP video stream, and each packet can be restored to its original raster location if desired. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Max ANC packets per RTP packet

today: RFC 8331 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2018. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Ancillary Data in Professional Video
sections.content:
SMPTE ST 291-1 defines ancillary data (ANC data). It is sent in the ancillary space of serial digital video interfaces, the space outside the active video region that viewers actually see. That space roughly corresponds to the vertical and horizontal blanking periods of cathode ray tube displays. ANC data can carry time code, Closed Captioning and the Active Format Description (AFD).

This memo describes an RTP payload format for it. The payload can carry ANC data packets from any location in any SMPTE-defined SDI signal, and also ANC data packets that never came from an SDI signal. Enough information is included to restore the packets to their original locations in the raster at the decoder output, if that is wanted.

The payload can be used by itself or alongside RTP video formats. It was designed to fit with RFC 4175 (uncompressed video) and RFC 5371 (JPEG 2000 video). Its data model is based on SMPTE ST 2038, which carries ANC data in an MPEG-2 Transport Stream.

The Ancillary Data Flag (ADF) word is not carried. It may be specified by the document defining the interconnecting digital video interface; otherwise SMPTE ST 291-1 gives a default.
sections.plainLanguage: Video has hidden side notes, like subtitles and clock times, tucked outside the picture. This RFC explains how to mail those notes over the internet, with or without the picture.

sections.title: The RTP Packet Layout
sections.content:
An RTP packet starts with the normal RTP header, interpreted as in RFC 3550, followed by the ANC payload header and then one or more ANC data packets. The RFC's example shows two ANC data packets, on lines 9 and 10 of the SDI raster, with four and five 10-bit words of user data. It notes that few real ANC packets are this small. The term network byte order refers to the Data Transmission Order in Appendix B of RFC 791.

Two RTP header fields have specific meanings here. The timestamp is the sampling instant of the frame (progressive video) or field (interlaced video) that the ANC data belongs to. An RTP packet MUST NOT hold ANC data from more than one frame or field, and all packets for the same frame or field MUST carry the same timestamp. If the sampling instant is not a whole number of clock ticks, the value is truncated to the next lowest integer.

The marker bit set to 1 marks the last ANC data RTP packet for a frame (progressive) or field (interlaced).
sections.plainLanguage: Each envelope says which picture its notes belong to, and the last envelope for a picture has a flag raised so the receiver knows nothing else is coming for that picture.

sections.title: Payload Header and ANC Packet Fields
sections.content:
The payload header has an Extended Sequence Number (16 bits, the same as in RFC 4175), a Length (16 bits, the octets of payload counted from the first ANC packet's C bit, including all word_align fields) and an ANC_Count (8 bits). One RTP packet cannot carry more than 255 ANC data packets; more can go in extra RTP packets with the same timestamp but different sequence numbers. An ANC_Count of 0 means no ANC packets, and then Length is also 0.

The 2-bit F field signals the field in interlaced video: 0b00 means progressive or no field, 0b10 the first field, 0b11 the second field. The value 0b01 is not valid, and receivers SHOULD ignore an ANC packet with it. Then 22 reserved bits of zero keep the first ANC header 32-bit aligned.

Each ANC data packet then MUST have these header fields: C (1 bit, set to 1 for the color-difference channel), Line_Number (11 bits), Horizontal_Offset (12 bits, measured in 10-bit words from the start of active video), S (1 bit) and StreamNum (7 bits). When S is 1, StreamNum MUST carry the source data stream number minus one. Special Line_Number and Horizontal_Offset values mean generic regions, for example 0x7FF with 0xFFF means no specific location.

After the header come DID, SDID, Data_Count, the User_Data_Words and a Checksum_Word, all 10-bit words as in SMPTE ST 291-1. The checksum is the nine least significant bits of the sum of the DID, SDID, Data_Count and user data words, with bit b9 the inverse of bit b8. Each ANC packet ends with word_align zero bits to fill the last 32-bit word, even for the last packet in an RTP packet, but not when there are zero ANC packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note carries a label for where it sat in the picture, which stream it came from, what kind of note it is, how long it is, and a check number. Padding makes every note end on a neat boundary.

sections.title: The video/smpte291 Media Type
sections.content:
The payload is identified by the video/smpte291 media type, registered under RFC 4855 using the template of RFC 6838. It sits in the video tree because ANC data is expected to be used with video. IANA has registered it in the Media Types registry.

The required parameter Rate is the RTP timestamp clock rate. If an ANC stream goes with an RTP video stream, the rates SHOULD be the same so ANC packets can be matched to the right frame or field. Otherwise a 90 kHz rate SHOULD be used.

Two parameters are optional. DID_SDID says that all ANC packets in the stream have particular DID and SDID values; Type 1 packets, which have no SDID, are labeled SDID=0x00. Without it, the types can only be found by inspecting the packets. VPID_Code is an integer taken from byte 1 of the Video Payload ID in SMPTE ST 352; for example, 132 refers to SMPTE ST 292-1 720-line video payloads on a 1.5 Gb/s (nominal) serial digital interface.

The type is defined only for transfer via RTP; transport within other framing protocols is not defined.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope gets an official name tag so everyone recognizes what is inside. Optional stickers say which kinds of notes are inside and what kind of video cable they came from.

sections.title: Describing and Negotiating Streams with SDP
sections.content:
The media type maps into SDP following RFC 4855: video goes in the m= line, smpte291 goes in a=rtpmap followed by a slash and the rate, and the optional parameters go in an a=fmtp line as a semicolon-separated list. DID and SDID values SHALL be written in hexadecimal with a 0x prefix. For example, EIA 608 Closed Caption data is DID_SDID={0x61,0x02} and AFD/Bar Data is DID_SDID={0x41,0x05}. Several DID_SDID parameters can be given, and they imply no ordering. VPID_Code appears at most once.

To tie an ANC stream to a video stream, implementers MAY group the m lines using the FID semantics of RFC 5888. In the offer/answer model of RFC 3264, an offerer MAY list ANC streams with specific DID_SDID parameters. The answerer MAY accept all or a subset, decline by setting the port to 0, or remove the payload type when the stream shares a media section with video. For declarative SDP, nothing specific is defined, and the SDP configuration MUST be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the notes are sent, both sides exchange a short description of what will be sent. The receiver can say yes to all of it, some of it, or none.

sections.title: Sending and Rebuilding the Signal
sections.content:
When rebuilding an SDI signal, ANC packets should be placed using the C, Line_Number and Horizontal_Offset fields and must follow Section 7 of SMPTE ST 291-1, which covers where initial ANC data may go and keeping ANC packet sequences contiguous so that the resulting packets are valid. VPID_Code can tell receivers the type of the originating interface, and StreamNum says which stream a packet can be placed in.

Senders SHOULD transmit available ANC packets as soon as practical to reduce end-to-end latency. One millisecond is given as a reasonable upper bound between a packet becoming available and an RTP payload containing it being sent. ANC packets with a specific location SHOULD be sent in raster scan order, both within an RTP packet and over time.
sections.plainLanguage: Send notes quickly, in the same order they appeared on the page, and put each back in the same spot when you rebuild the picture.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packets are subject to the security considerations of RFC 3550 and any RTP profile in use. Following RFC 7202, the payload format itself does not mandate a security solution; applications SHOULD use one or more appropriately strong mechanisms, and guidance is in RFC 7201.

To avoid buffer overflow attacks, receivers SHOULD check that the length of each ANC packet (from Data_Count) fits the type given by DID and SDID. They SHOULD also check the Checksum_Word, though it is unlikely to protect against a directed attack. Receivers that simply move ANC bits into SDI (re-embedders) should still do these checks, because bad packets could confuse downstream systems and be used for denial of service. They SHOULD also verify that Line_Number and Horizontal_Offset point to a legal ANC area of the output video format.
sections.plainLanguage: A careful receiver checks each envelope's size and check number before using it, so a sneaky or damaged one cannot cause trouble.

fields.name: Extended Sequence Number
fields.desc: High-order bits of the extended 32-bit sequence number.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets of ANC payload, counted from the C bit of the first ANC packet header.

fields.name: ANC_Count
fields.desc: Number of ANC data packets in this payload, at most 255.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Field signaling: 0b00, 0b10 or 0b11; 0b01 is not valid.

fields.name: reserved
fields.desc: Zero bits that keep the next header 32-bit aligned.

fields.name: Line_Number
fields.desc: Interface line where the ANC packet sits.

fields.name: Horizontal_Offset
fields.desc: Position relative to the start of active video, in 10-bit words.

fields.name: StreamNum
fields.desc: Source data stream number minus one, when S is 1.

items.label: No specific line
items.desc: Without specific line location within the field or frame.

items.label: Generic region
items.desc: Any line from the second line after the switching line (SMPTE RP 168) to the last line before active video.

items.label: Line too large
items.desc: A line number larger than 11 bits can represent, if needed for future formats.
